nameStory: This plant gets its descriptive name from the small hairs that grow right at the joints where its leaves meet the stem - these 'hairy joints' make it stand out from its smooth-stemmed cousins. The 'meadow-parsnip' part comes from its membership in the carrot family and its preference for open, grassy areas, though it's not actually related to the parsnip you might grow in your garden.
description: Hairy-jointed meadow-parsnip is a perennial wildflower in the carrot family that produces clusters of bright yellow, umbrella-shaped flowers. This native plant typically grows as a shorter herb compared to its relatives, reaching modest heights in open areas. Like other members of the carrot family, it has the characteristic flat-topped flower clusters called umbels that look like tiny yellow umbrellas. It's quite rare in New England, representing the northern edge of its natural range.

idTips.label: Stem Joints
idTips.description: Look for small, fine hairs right where the leaves attach to the stem - run your finger along these joints to feel the soft, fuzzy texture that gives this plant its name

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow umbrella-shaped clusters (umbels) that sit flat on top like tiny parasols - each small flower has 5 petals and the whole cluster feels slightly rough to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A relatively short, upright perennial herb that tends to be more compact than other meadow-parsnips, growing in small patches or individual plants

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves divided into smaller leaflets, with a fresh, slightly spicy scent when crushed - typical of the carrot family

habitat: In New England, this extremely rare plant would be found in open meadows, prairie remnants, or woodland edges with rich, well-drained soil. It prefers sunny to partially shaded locations in areas that aren't too wet or too dry. Given its rarity here, it's most likely to appear in specialized habitats like restored prairies or nature preserves.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge and the plant begins its growth cycle, with fresh green foliage appearing in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time when the distinctive bright yellow umbel clusters are most visible and the hairy joints are easiest to observe on actively growing stems.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seeds develop, while leaves may begin to yellow and die back as the plant prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground as a perennial, with no above-ground parts visible until the following spring.

funFact: This plant is so rare in New England that it has been observed only once in our entire region - making any sighting a truly special botanical discovery that would excite plant enthusiasts across the Northeast!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other yellow-flowered members of the carrot family, but the hairy joints where leaves meet the stem are your foolproof identification feature - most similar plants have completely smooth stems at these connection points.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, meadow-parsnips aren't actually parsnips at all - they're just distant relatives in the large carrot family. This naming can be confusing since the carrot family includes everything from carrots and parsnips to poison hemlock, so never assume edibility based on family relationships.
compareHints: Since this is the only Thaspium species recorded in New England, compare it with other yellow carrot family flowers like wild parsnip or golden alexanders. The key difference is those hairy stem joints - wild parsnip has completely smooth, often purple-tinged stems, while golden alexanders lacks the distinctive fuzzy texture at leaf attachment points.
